The high tide empire is being destroyed, and Egypt is under attack. Egypt will survive the invasions by the sea peoples but will be exhausted afterward, losing its global power status. In this valley, refugees fleeing from the steps, Mesopotamia, will overwhelm the area. Mesopotamia is the most resilient of the four major civilizations due to constant warfare throughout its history.

Egypt has natural boundaries provided by the desert and the Red Sea. China also has natural boundaries, but Mesopotamia does not; it's a flat land making it easy for mountain people and outsiders to invade and build new empires. Throughout Mesopotamian history, there have been three major empires: the Aadian Empire, the Babylonian Empire, and the Assyrian Empire, none lasting more than a couple of hundred years due to intense competition.

The big question is why this world might collapse suddenly, similar to how the bronze age world collapsed. Many scholars compare our heavily globalized world to that ancient one, wondering if it too could face sudden collapse despite many countries getting wealthy. The argument today is about capital's nature: a protocapitalistic system allows for rapid growth but also rapid collapse.

Capital has three characteristics: universality (everyone wants and values it), storability (you can store wealth in it), and mobility (it can be transported with little cost). Examples include grain, cattle, and slaves. Grain never became capital due to its instability and difficulty in transportation. Cattle is better but still not ideal for storage. Slaves were a basic form of capital but unstable.

Bronze, however, became the first real universal currency because it was highly valued, stored a lot of value, and could be moved easily, leading to rapid globalization akin to today's US dollar facilitating global capitalism.
